heading: Chapter 1: Understanding Container Orchestration
content: Containers changed how we package software, but managing hundreds of them requires orchestration. In this chapter, we'll build a mental model for why orchestration matters and what problems it solves. By the end, you'll understand the gap between 'I can run a container' and 'I can run a production service.'

heading: 1.1 From Containers to Clusters
content: Let's start with a scenario you've probably lived: your app works perfectly in a single container on your laptop. But in production, you need multiple replicas, health checks, rolling updates, and service discovery. As we'll see in Chapter 2, Kubernetes solves these problems with a declarative model.

heading: Chapter 2: Kubernetes Core Concepts
content: Now that we understand the problem space (from Chapter 1), let's learn the building blocks. Kubernetes has a steep learning curve because it introduces many abstractions at once. We'll tackle them one at a time, showing how each solves a specific problem from our earlier discussion.

heading: 2.1 Pods and Containers
content: A Pod is the smallest deployable unit — not a container, but a group of containers that share a network namespace. Before reading further, make sure you're comfortable with Linux namespaces.

heading: Chapter 3: Networking and Services
content: With Pods running (as we set up in Chapter 2), the next challenge is communication. How do Pods find each other? This chapter builds on the networking foundation from 2.1.

heading: API Reference
content: Complete reference for the Kubernetes API resources organized alphabetically.

heading: ConfigMap
content: A ConfigMap is an API object used to store non-confidential data in key-value pairs. Pods can consume ConfigMaps as environment variables, command-line arguments, or as configuration files in a volume.

heading: DaemonSet
content: A DaemonSet ensures that all or some nodes run a copy of a Pod. As nodes are added to the cluster, Pods are added to them. As nodes are removed, those Pods are garbage collected.

heading: Deployment
content: A Deployment provides declarative updates for Pods and ReplicaSets. You describe a desired state and the Deployment controller changes the actual state to the desired state at a controlled rate.

heading: Ingress
content: An Ingress is an API object that manages external access to services in a cluster, typically HTTP. Ingress may provide load balancing, SSL termination, and name-based virtual hosting.

heading: Service
content: A Service is an abstract way to expose an application running on a set of Pods as a network service. Kubernetes gives Pods their own IP addresses and a single DNS name for a set of Pods.

heading: StatefulSet
content: StatefulSet is the workload API object used to manage stateful applications. Manages the deployment and scaling of a set of Pods with guarantees about ordering and uniqueness.
